idiom_name: location value = focused subtree + reversed path to the root
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the tree as a closed recursive type, then derive a matching context type with one frame per level - a frame keeps the parent's own data plus the siblings on either side of the hole - and make the location the pair (focus, context chain). Navigation pushes a frame (down/left/right) or pops one and reconstructs the parent (up); edits replace the focus or splice a sibling and return a new location; a single rebuild (top/root) folds the context back into a tree. Keep the context type derived from the node type so navigation and rebuild stay total, report boundary moves in the return type, and never mutate a node: every operation returns a new value so earlier locations keep denoting the version they were taken from.
code_sketch:
type Tree = Leaf of item | Branch of Tree list
type Path = Top | Node of Tree list * Path * Tree list   (* siblings either side *)
type Loc  = Loc of Tree * Path                            (* focus + context *)

down (Loc (Branch (h :: _), p)) = Loc (h, Node ([], p, []))        (* push *)
up   (Loc (t, Node (l, p, r)))  = Loc (Branch (rev l @ t :: r), p) (* pop + rebuild *)
top  (Loc (t, Top))             = t                                 (* one O(depth) step *)
pitfalls: Rebuilding the parent on every step of a long walk duplicates work; batch the edits and rebuild once at the top.
Modelling the focus as an index into a mutable node instead of a value re-introduces exactly the aliasing the pattern removes.
Boundary moves (up at the root, left at the first sibling) are partial: put that in the return type instead of leaving it undefined.
A context type that is not derived from the node type drifts: a new node case silently makes navigation incomplete.

Keeping the left-sibling list in parent order makes every sideways move reverse it, so navigation silently costs O(width) per step; hold left siblings reversed (as a stack) so left/right push and pop in O(1).

The context encodes exactly one path, so a subtree shared by several parents has one location per path: editing through one occurrence leaves the location taken along the other path denoting the old version, and rebuilding from each path duplicates the shared node instead of updating it - zipper a tree, not a DAG.
